paper.title: Evolving Excellence: Automated Optimization of LLM-based Agents
paper.central_claim: Artemis, a no-code evolutionary platform with semantically-aware genetic operators, jointly optimizes LLM-agent configurations (prompts, tool descriptions, parameters) without architectural changes, improving four agents (ALE +13.6% acceptance, Mini-SWE +10.1%, CrewAI -39.1% tokens, MathTales +37.3% accuracy).

evidence.quote: treat components in isolation, missing critical interdependencies
evidence.support_explanation: Author gap: existing optimizers treat components in isolation; the joint-interdependence claim is the stated motivation.

evidence.quote: Given only a benchmark script and natural language goals, Artemis automatically discovers configurable components, extracts performance signals from execution logs, and evolves configurations without requiring architectural modifications.
evidence.support_explanation: Defines the object (agent configuration) and the feedback (benchmark script + logs); black-box, architecture-agnostic.

evidence.quote: the platform uses LLM-based semantic understanding to evaluate fitness based on benchmark results
evidence.support_explanation: Fitness is partly produced by an LLM from natural-language goals rather than a fixed formula; the exact scoring function is not given.

evidence.quote: using heuristics refined through extensive optimization runs
evidence.support_explanation: Key orchestration heuristics (when to run expensive evaluations, confidence calibration, operator design) are proprietary and not specified.

evidence.quote: Evolves individual components independently using genetic algorithms (GA).
evidence.support_explanation: Local optimization: per-component GA with LLM mutation/crossover, for components without strong interdependencies.

evidence.quote: Uses Bayesian optimization to find optimal combinations when components interact.
evidence.support_explanation: Global optimization over component versions; the 'interdependence' premise is operationalised here but not ablated.

evidence.quote: However, optimization was performed exclusively for acceptance rate; performance and rank metrics were automatically calculated by the benchmark but never used in optimization logic, improving only indirectly through better algorithmic choices for correctness.
evidence.support_explanation: ALE configuration is optimized on the acceptance rate of the same 40-problem benchmark on which it is reported.

evidence.quote: During the optimisation process, we extract a subset of 50 problems from the benchmark as the validation set, select the configuration achieving the best metric performance, and then evaluate this selected version against the baseline on a larger set of 300 problems
evidence.support_explanation: Only validation/evaluation split in the paper; overlap between the 50 and the 300 problems is not stated.

evidence.quote: Genetic algorithm with two generations and a population size of 3.
evidence.support_explanation: The MathTales evolutionary search is tiny (2 generations x 3 candidates), so improvement likely comes from replacing a very simplistic prompt rather than from search.

evidence.quote: While neither reached statistical significance at α = 0.05 \alpha=0.05 ( p = 0.10 p=0.10 for both)
evidence.support_explanation: ALE gains (0.660 -> 0.750 prompt, 0.722 search) are not statistically significant; 95% CIs overlap.

evidence.quote: The optimization process required 411.2 hours for prompt optimization and 260.5 hours for search optimization
evidence.support_explanation: Wall-clock optimization cost for ALE (671.7 h in total, see Sec 7).

evidence.quote: The Mini-SWE Agent demonstrated a statistically significant 10.1% performance improvement (p < 0.05) using the Mann-Whitney U test
evidence.support_explanation: Mini-SWE improvement is significant by the authors' test (0.891 -> 0.981 in Table 3), single optimization run.

evidence.quote: The optimization completed in 9 hours across three generations with a population size of 3.
evidence.support_explanation: Mini-SWE evolutionary search is likewise tiny (3 generations x 3 candidates).

evidence.quote: This came with a small but statistically significant 7.3% decrease in the average rate of correct problems (0.82 → \rightarrow 0.76, p = 0.027 =0.027 ).
evidence.support_explanation: The 39.1% token reduction was bought with an accuracy decrease (0.82 -> 0.76, p=0.027); in the 50x6 design the decrease is n.s. (p=0.277).

evidence.quote: intentionally failed at zero expense
evidence.support_explanation: Cost reduction is partly obtained by token limits that fail expensive problems at no cost: the cost metric is satisfied through a trade, not through efficiency alone.

evidence.quote: Across three repeated runs on the evaluation set, the optimised agent achieves an average completion rate of 0.917 versus 0.796 for the baseline (+15.2%) and an average accuracy of 0.81 versus 0.59 (+37.3%).
evidence.support_explanation: Largest effect: Qwen2.5-7B agent, 3 repeated evaluation runs on 300 problems, p<0.001; baseline prompt was 'simplistic'.

evidence.quote: optimizations may be specific to evaluation datasets rather than universally applicable
evidence.support_explanation: Authors concede that gains may be benchmark-specific (project-level Mini-SWE results from +7.2 to -0.1 points).

evidence.quote: establishing robust validation setups that avoid overfitting to specific benchmarks remains challenging
evidence.support_explanation: Authors acknowledge the overfitting/validation risk.

evidence.quote: Comparative analysis of LLM agent optimization frameworks
evidence.support_explanation: Comparison with APE, PromptBreeder, ADAS, AFlow, AlphaCodium, GEPA, ShinkaEvolve is a qualitative table (Scope/Generality/Semantic/Scalable ratings assigned by the authors); no method was run as a baseline.

evidence.quote: The most striking pattern is the relationship between initial configuration quality and optimization success.
evidence.support_explanation: Authors attribute gains to weak, generic starting prompts; the baseline is not a tuned human prompt.

evidence.quote: While the complete Artemis platform setup cannot be shared, the provided code allows practitioners to examine our agent implementations and verify the reported performance improvements.
evidence.support_explanation: The optimizer itself (Artemis, TurinTech) is not released; only the four target agents are.

evidence.quote: The ALE Agent required 671.7 total hours across all optimization experiments, representing substantial resource investment.
evidence.support_explanation: Cost of optimization reported in hours; monetary or token cost of the evolution runs is not reported.

evidence.quote: cheap evaluators (LLM-based scoring, static analysis) filter candidates quickly, while expensive evaluators (full benchmark runs) validate only promising configurations.
evidence.support_explanation: Hierarchical evaluation: LLM-scored proxy filters before benchmark execution; proxy-to-real rank transfer is not checked.

evidence.quote: For prompt optimization, we employ evolutionary prompt engineering to evolve prompts from simple Chain-of-Thought (CoT) approaches to include sophisticated self-correction checklists.
evidence.support_explanation: ALE prompt optimisation is one run …

evidence.quote: For search optimization, we apply genetic algorithms with advanced search strategies (such as beam search and taboo memory) for systematic exploration of the solution space.
evidence.support_explanation: … and search-strategy optimisation a separate run (reported separately in Fig. 6): the joint multi-component optimisation that answers the paper's stated gap is not exercised in this case.

evidence.quote: Artemis incorporates novel mutation and crossover operators specifically designed for natural language components
evidence.support_explanation: The claimed novel mechanism; its prompts, algorithm and selection rule are never specified.

evidence.quote: Finally, validate improvements on held-out data to ensure generalization beyond training benchmarks.
evidence.support_explanation: The authors' own guideline, not followed for ALE, Mini-SWE or CrewAI.

signatures.object: Black-box agent configuration: system prompts, tool descriptions, YAML parameters/templates, search-strategy code (ALE), model/temperature settings
signatures.information: Benchmark script and results, execution logs, natural-language optimization goals; agent internals are not modified
signatures.operation: Discover configurable components by semantic search; evolve them with LLM-ensemble mutation/crossover (local GA per component) or Bayesian optimization over component-version combinations (global)
signatures.output: An optimized configuration file that replaces the baseline
signatures.conditions: A runnable benchmark with an objective metric; headroom in the baseline prompts; budget of tens to hundreds of hours
signatures.feedback: Benchmark outcomes/logs; LLM-based scoring as a cheap proxy before full benchmark runs
signatures.selection_rule: Highest fitness (LLM-interpreted from natural-language goals) after hierarchical evaluation; exact rule and operators not disclosed (E003, E004)
signatures.selection_data: Same benchmark as reported for ALE and (apparently) Mini-SWE/CrewAI; 50-problem validation vs 300-problem evaluation for MathTales (E007, E008)
signatures.persistence: Final configuration file reused in deployment ('persist across future deployments')
signatures.later_use: Deployed agent uses the new configuration; no further evolution read-back
signatures.claimed_effect: ALE +13.6% acceptance (n.s.), Mini-SWE +10.1% (sig.), CrewAI -39.1% tokens with -7.3% accuracy, MathTales +37.3% accuracy
signatures.failure_boundary: Little headroom if the baseline is already tuned; benchmark-specific gains (project-level range +7.2 to -0.1); expensive for large evaluations

signatures.object: Fitness signal and evaluation schedule of the optimizer
signatures.information: Natural-language goals; benchmark metrics; LLM judgements
signatures.operation: LLM interprets benchmark results against goals to produce fitness; cheap LLM/static filters precede full benchmark runs
signatures.conditions: Proxy must rank-correlate with true benchmark score (unchecked)
signatures.failure_boundary: Cost metric can be satisfied by failing expensive problems (E015)

gap.author_gap: Agent optimization methods optimize isolated components (prompts, workflows) or need architectural access; few unified, architecture-agnostic end-to-end frameworks exploit execution logs.
gap.checked_gap: Isolated-component optimizers exist (APE, PromptBreeder, GEPA, DSPy) and joint prompt+tool+parameter tuning is plausibly useful, but the paper gives no measurement that component interdependence limits isolated optimization, and its comparison with neighbours is a self-rated qualitative table (E019).
gap.lineage: APE/PromptBreeder (prompt evolution) -> GEPA (Pareto reflective prompt evolution), DSPy (prompt/pipeline compilation), ADAS/AFlow (workflow code search) -> Artemis (proprietary semantic GA + Bayesian optimization over agent configuration).
gap.closest_adjacent: GEPA and DSPy (closest in object and feedback), ADAS/AFlow (agent structure), ShinkaEvolve (LLM evolutionary code); none re-run here and none fixed locally as source text.
gap.residue: Whether joint optimization beats isolated or simple LLM-rewrite baselines; transfer of tuned configurations across tasks and LLMs; held-out validity of gains.
gap.stakes: Weeks of manual configuration effort per agent.
gap.method_response: Black-box platform with semantic mutation/crossover, local and global search, hierarchical evaluation.
gap.remaining_gap: No ablation of joint vs isolated or semantic vs plain operators, no comparison with another optimizer, no held-out split for most agents, proprietary operators.
gap.unresolved: Neighbour papers' reported numbers and claims not fixed as local sources.

rs_pattern.reason: Opus confirms son55. The executed operation is LLM-operator evolutionary + Bayesian search over agent configuration text/parameters against benchmark fitness. Run precedent cal-dev GrIPS (instruction search, H13) and r04b EvoAgentX ruled outside_taxonomy: generative_process_redesign needs a fixed component of an iterative/staged generative procedure; agent prompts/configs are model input, and 'free a fixed component' would then cover any optimizer (sol's match). Also rejected: heterogeneous_decomposition, relax_discrete_search_to_continuous (BO over discrete versions is not a relaxation), decompose_and_delegate (cheap→expensive evaluation is scheduling, not delegation to a sound solver), adapt_via_conditioning (per-task search over the conditioning text, no cross-task conditioning; GrIPS ruling). Fully evaluated regardless.

matches.condition_checks: step1 genome and neighbourhood fixed: met (prompts, tool descriptions, parameters; search-strategy code for ALE); step2 fitness defined before searching: partial (benchmark metrics chosen per agent, but fitness is LLM-interpreted from natural-language goals); step3 scoring vs reporting separation: unmet for ALE/Mini-SWE/CrewAI as described, partial for MathTales (50 vs 300, overlap unstated); step4 explicit budget and cost: partial (hours, $24-26 per ALE run, no total tokens or $ for evolution); step5 show what the search adds against greedy/random/no-search: unmet. F1 generic loop on new domains: present as the contribution is platform application.

assessment.strongest_supported_claim: For three of four agents, configurations produced by the Artemis platform score higher than the authors' original configurations on the benchmarks they were tuned on (significantly for Mini-SWE and MathTales; not for ALE; CrewAI trades accuracy for tokens).
assessment.cannot_say: That joint optimization or the semantic operators cause the gains; that Artemis outperforms any other optimizer or a plain LLM rewrite; held-out or cross-task validity; reproducibility of the optimizer.
unresolved: Selection/test overlap for Mini-SWE/CrewAI/MathTales; mutation prompts and operator design; evolution token cost.
assessment.reproduction_note: All results are author-reported; nothing re-run by us.

G.reason: Both seats 2; re-checked. Manual tuning effort and isolated-component optimisation are real limitations, and GEPA/DSPy/ADAS/AFlow are named, but only via a self-rated table; no measurement that component interdependence is the bottleneck.

M.reason: Opus sides with son55. The paper's response to its own gap (interdependent components) is joint search with novel semantic operators, but the operators are never specified (opus:O03), the core heuristics are proprietary (son55:E004), and in the headline ALE case prompts and search strategies are optimised in separate runs (opus:O01, opus:O02), so the joint-optimisation logic is not exercised. What remains is generic LLM evolution with a generic validity argument and no distinguishing prediction — below the anchor-2 'specific mechanism with partial causal account' (cf. r04b EvoAgentX M=1). sol's 2 credited the GA/BO/cheap-filter outline, which X already scores.

X.reason: Both seats 2; re-checked. Workflow (setup → discovery → local GA / global BO → hierarchical evaluation) and boundaries (headroom, metric clarity, cost) are described with before/after configs; operators, fitness extraction, selection rule, retention/rollback are unspecified or proprietary; populations of 3 for 2–3 generations.

E.measurement.reason: Both seats 2; re-checked. Official metrics for ALE-Bench, SWE-Perf and GSM8K; but fitness is LLM-interpreted, the CrewAI 'reporting analyst' that evaluates correctness is itself among the optimised prompts (App. Fig. 13), and the token objective was partly met by intentionally failing expensive problems.

E.causality.reason: Both seats 1; re-checked. Only before/after comparisons against the authors' own generic initial configs; no other optimiser, random/greedy/no-search or plain LLM-rewrite baseline, and no ablation of any Artemis component.

E.holdout.reason: Opus sides with son55. Three of four headline results have no stated selection/reporting separation (ALE tuned and reported on the same 40 problems; Mini-SWE and CrewAI splits undescribed); MathTales has a 50-validation / 300-evaluation design with unstated overlap on public GSM8K. The authors themselves flag benchmark overfitting and recommend held-out validation they did not run (opus:O04). One partial split does not reach anchor 2 for the paper's cross-agent claim.

E.statistics.reason: Both seats 2; re-checked (A2 ladder: test-set CIs and repeated evaluation, no variance across optimisation runs). Non-significant ALE (p=0.10) and the CrewAI accuracy drop are disclosed; one evolutionary run per agent.

E.cost.reason: Both seats 2; re-checked. Optimisation hours (671.7 h ALE, 9 h Mini-SWE) and per-run dollar cost are reported; evolution token/$ cost, cheap-proxy cost and matched budgets are not; MathTales hardware cost ignored.
